title: the mountain ahead
hookLine: the mountain ahead; Rumi's field beyond our ideas of right and wrong (a paraphrase; the well-known wording is a modern, copyrighted version)
tomorrow: Marcus doesn't want to get up

cards: Three weeks ago you took one breath with a bell. Today you've got twenty words on your strand, and you're standing at the edge of the first camp, looking up at the mountain ahead. So for the last word of camp one, a poet.
Not a rule, not a technique. A person. A Persian poet whose lines get shared on phones every day, often with his name on them and his world left off.

teach.b: Jalal al-Din Rumi was born in the eastern Persian world, in what's now Afghanistan or Tajikistan; the old biographies disagree on the town.
His family moved west, ahead of the Mongol invasions, and settled in Konya, in today's Turkey. He became a respected Muslim scholar and teacher, steeped in the Qur'an, and his poetry is full of it.
Popular versions often leave that out.
Then, already a grown man with students of his own, he met a wandering mystic called Shams of Tabriz, and his life turned over.
The old biographies say the friendship was so intense that his students grew jealous, and Shams eventually disappeared. Out of that loss came an ocean of poems.
His great work, the Masnavi, begins with a reed flute crying. It was cut from the reed bed, and every note it plays is longing to go back.
There's a well-known saying credited to Rumi about a field, somewhere beyond our ideas of doing wrong and doing right, where he'll meet you.
The wording most people share is a modern English version, not his, and scholars aren't sure how closely it follows the Persian.
So, paraphrased and honestly labeled: a place past the arguing, where two people can simply meet. That's where camp one has been walking you. Meant to be.
Company. Rumi. Twenty-one words from many homes, and not one of them asked you to believe anything.

how: Rumi's poems are read and sung across the Muslim world and far beyond; in the Mevlevi order founded by his followers, his verses accompany the sema, the turning ceremony people call whirling.

games.q: you're a reed, cut from the reed bed and made into a flute. in the opening of the Masnavi, what does your music say?
o: that you're glad to be free of the marsh.
that you long to go back where you came from.
games.why: the flute cries for the reed bed it was cut from. for Rumi, that longing is the soul's longing to go home.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, picture a wide open field, early evening.
No arguments there. Nobody keeping score. Then let one person come to mind that you've been at odds with, even a little.
Don't fix anything. Just picture them walking into the same field, from the other side, and let there be room for both of you.

wordCard.voice: Rumi. A Persian Muslim poet and teacher from Konya, and the voice of longing to go home. Twenty-first word, and the end of camp one.

orig.note: Persian, ney: the reed flute that opens Rumi's Masnavi, still played in Mevlevi ceremonies today.

carryVoice: Your line: meet me there. That's camp one, finished; tomorrow, camp two opens with a Roman emperor who doesn't want to get out of bed.
